videoTitle: Alarms to AI: Trigger AWS DevOps Agent With EventBridge & Webhooks
videoDescription:
An alarm at 2 AM wakes a human. In this episode we make it wake AWS DevOps Agent first: a real CloudWatch alarm starts an investigation by itself, with no code, and the agent follows your own runbook.

In this episode you will:
• Build an alarm users would feel: ALB HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, Sum over 1 minute ≥ 10, missing data as good
• Add latency (p95) and memory alarms from the CLI
• Create an Agent Space webhook with an API key, and see the incident schema it expects
• Build an EventBridge rule (Advanced builder): checkout-* alarms in ALARM → API destination with a bearer key, plus an input transformer that turns the alarm into an incident
• See the HMAC alternative: a Lambda that signs timestamp:body (we tested it: body-only signatures get a 403)
• Fire a drill with set-alarm-state and watch the investigation appear by itself, then cancel it
• Teach the agent your runbook with a custom skill
• Find the native integrations: Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, Slack, Datadog

Why not a built-in trigger? DevOps Agent's own triggers only run on schedules, so events go through the webhook.

Cost: the drill ran under two minutes of agent time (about $0.90 at $0.0083 per second). Alarms are $0.10 per month each, and the EventBridge connection secret is about $0.40 per month.

videoTitle: Your Bash Scripts Fail Silently. Fix It With One Line (set -euo pipefail)
videoDescription:
Most production incidents caused by shell scripts are not crashes - they are scripts that kept running after something went wrong. Step by step, we break a real-looking backup script, then fix it with Bash strict mode: what each of the three options does, shown with a real failure, and the gotchas to know before adding it everywhere.

▶ Full series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLChbU3Wyo8x8

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:13 The plan
0:33 The silent failure
1:24 The fix: one line
1:51 Option -e
2:19 Option -u
2:54 Option pipefail
3:24 Recap and gotchas

Transcript:
Here is a scary fact. By default, when a command in a Bash script fails, Bash just keeps going. Let's watch that break a backup script, and then fix it with one single line.

== The plan ==
Here is the plan.
First, we break a real looking backup script.
Then we fix it with one line.
That line has three options. We see each one catch a different failure.
And we finish with the gotchas to know before you add it everywhere.

== The silent failure ==
Here is a backup script that looks reasonable. Let's read it.
It goes into the data folder, slash data slash app.
Then it cleans the old files in the current folder. In our demo, it only prints the delete command, and the name of the folder it would run in. Nothing is really deleted.
And it reports success.
On this server, slash data slash app does not exist. Let's run the script.
$ bash backup.sh
Look at the first line: cd failed. But the script kept going. It would have deleted everything in demo, the folder we happened to be in. Not the data folder.
And what exit code did it return?
$ echo "exit code: $?"

== The fix: one line ==
The fix is called Bash strict mode. One line, three options. Let's read them one by one.
Dash e: stop the script as soon as a command fails.
Dash u: using a variable that was never set is an error, instead of an empty string.
And dash o pipefail: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last one.

== Option -e ==
Here is the same script, with one extra line at the top. Nothing else changed.
Same broken server. Let's run it.
$ bash backup-strict.sh
This time the script stops right at the failed cd. No cleaning, no success message.
And the exit code?
$ echo "exit code: $?"
One. Now your scheduler, or your CI pipeline, knows the backup failed.

== Option -u ==
Now option dash u. Look at this cleanup script. There is a typo: B U L I D instead of B U I L D.
$ cat cleanup.sh
Without strict mode, the misspelled variable is just empty. So the path becomes slash cache, at the root of the disk.
$ bash cleanup.sh
This version has set dash u. Same typo.
$ bash cleanup-strict.sh
Bash refuses to continue, and tells you exactly which variable is not set.

== Option pipefail ==
Last option: pipefail. There is no file called app dot log here, so grep fails. But we pipe it into sort and head. Let's see the exit code of the whole pipeline.
$ grep ERROR app.log | sort | head -3; echo "exit code: $?"
Zero. By default, a pipeline returns the exit code of its last command, head, and head was fine.
Now with pipefail turned on. Exact same pipeline.
$ set -o pipefail; grep ERROR app.log | sort | head -3; echo "exit code: $?"

(continues) The full transcript is in the captions: click ...more, then Show transcript.

videoTitle: Branch a 2TB Postgres database without copying it #postgres #cli #devops
videoDescription:
How do you get an isolated copy of a 2TB production Postgres database? Branch it. With the Xata CLI, we initialize a local folder to our org and project, then create two kinds of branches off the main production branch: a persistent branch that stays as long as you need it, and a scratch branch that's ephemeral and cleans itself up. Each one gets its own Postgres connection string and is fully isolated from production thanks to copy-on-write, so you can change schemas, drop tables, or add new ones without touching your live data.

videoTitle: Claude said it couldn't fix it. Exit code said success.
videoDescription:
I ran Claude Code 2.1.319 headless (claude -p) 10 times on a one-line bug, with file edits denied.
5 runs with the new permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting, 5 without. Same result every time.
Claude told the truth: "I couldn't fix it, the file is unchanged." 10 of 10.
But the process exited with code 0 and is_error: false. 10 of 10. Files changed: 0.
A CI step that only checks the exit code would call that a success.
My take: when an agent can be refused and keep going, check what changed (git diff), not the exit code.

Try it:
claude -p "Fix the bug in calc.py" --output-format json | jq '.permission_denials | length'
Anything above 0 means a tool call was refused. Fail your job on that, or on an empty git diff.

What's new in 2.1.319: permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting denies a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt, and the turn continues (terminal sessions, subagents, teammates).

Heads-up: my setup only. Claude Code 2.1.319, claude-sonnet-5-5, default permission mode, macOS, 10 runs. I didn't test interactive sessions. In headless mode the setting made no difference, because claude -p can't show a prompt anyway. The same release makes auto-mode refusals exit 1, but only when no safety check was available. Plain permission denials still exited 0 for me.

Sources & links
• Claude Code 2.1.319 changelog (primary source): https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md
• Release v2.1.319: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/releases/tag/v2.1.319
• Claude Code headless mode docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
• How I measured: 2 conditions x 5 runs, claude -p --permission-mode default, the same prompt. A run counts as fixed if calc.py actually changed. Exit code and the JSON result fields were recorded as-is.

videoTitle: Port Already in Use? Fix It
videoDescription:
Error: listen EADDRINUSE? Another program is still holding your port. Here's how to free it in seconds.

🔍 Find it: lsof -i :3000 shows the program and its PID
🛑 Stop it: kill PID (kill -9 PID forces it, but the program gets no cleanup, so use it last)
🔀 Or skip the fight: PORT=3001 npm start (works when your app reads the PORT variable)

🪟 On Windows: netstat -ano | findstr :3000, then taskkill /PID 4821 /F (use your own PID)

Commands shown are for macOS and Linux. The PID 4821 is a made-up example.

videoTitle: Permission Denied? chmod Explained
videoDescription:
bash: Permission denied? Your script isn't allowed to run. Here's what those rwx letters mean and how to fix it.

🔘 Every file has 3 switches: r (read), w (write), x (execute), set separately for you, your group and everyone else. ls -l shows them, like -rw-r--r--
✅ chmod +x deploy.sh turns on execute, so the script runs (usually becomes -rwxr-xr-x)
🔢 Numbers: r=4, w=2, x=1, added per group. 755 for scripts and folders, 644 for normal files

⚠️ Don't use chmod 777: it lets anyone on the machine change your file.

Concept: Unix file permissions and chmod (macOS and Linux).
deploy.sh and its output are made-up examples.

videoTitle: helm install --dry-run Doesn't Check Your Cluster ⚠️ #Shorts
videoDescription:
In Helm 4, a plain --dry-run is --dry-run=client. It renders your chart on your machine and never connects to the cluster, which is basically what helm template does.

helm template → renders locally, lookup returns empty
helm install --dry-run=client → renders locally, no cluster connection
helm install --dry-run=server → talks to the cluster, so lookup sees real data (needs a reachable cluster)

Tip: helm template for quick renders. --dry-run=server before you ship.
Bonus: on Helm 4, a bare --dry-run prints a warning that it's deprecated and should be replaced with --dry-run=client.

videoTitle: Who actually runs a Kubernetes cluster? ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops #cloudnative
videoDescription:
Who actually runs a cluster? There's no one at the wheel. Just a few programs, each with one small job. ⚓

🏢 The control plane is the harbour office.

📖 etcd is the log book, where the cluster's state is kept.

🔀 kube-proxy keeps the network rules for Services.

videoTitle: Docker Image vs Container
videoDescription:
Image or container? They're not the same thing. Think of a recipe and the dish you cook from it.

📦 An image is the recipe: your code plus everything it needs, frozen in read-only layers. Build it once with docker build -t myapp .
▶️ A container is that image, running: docker run myapp. One image can start many containers, like a class and its objects
🗑️ Containers are throwaway: docker rm -f removes one and every change made inside it. The image stays. Keep data you need in a volume

🔍 docker images lists your images, docker ps lists running containers (docker ps -a shows stopped ones too).

videoTitle: Top K Frequent Elements LeetCode for DevOps Log Analysis
videoDescription:
Count items with a dictionary, then take the k largest counts. Sorting is order n log n, a size-k heap is order n plus m log k, and bucketing by frequency is order n. For deterministic output, break ties by name.

Episode 2 of 6 in the series 'LeetCode Interview Questions for DevOps and SRE Engineers'.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Which error is the loudest?
0:42 The problem in our words
1:34 Brute force: count, then sort
2:19 Buckets and heaps
3:06 Worked trace
3:44 Complexity
4:31 Follow-up: break ties
5:18 topk in monitoring, and recap

QUICK ANSWERS
Q: How do you solve Top K Frequent Elements in linear time?
A: Count with a dictionary, then put each item in a bucket indexed by its count and read buckets from the highest count down until you have k items. This is order n time and order n space.

Q: When should you use a heap instead of buckets?
A: A heap of size k costs order n plus m log k for m distinct items, which is attractive when k is tiny. Python's heapq.nlargest and heapq.nsmallest are documented to return the n largest or smallest elements of an iterable.

Q: Does Prometheus have a top k operator?
A: Yes. The Prometheus documentation lists topk(k, v) as an aggregation operator that returns the largest k elements by sample value, with an example of the five instances with the highest memory consumption.

KEY FACTS AND SOURCES
- As of October 2026, LeetCode lists problem 347 as Top K Frequent Elements and problem 692 as Top K Frequent Words.
- As of October 2026, the Prometheus documentation lists topk(k, v) as returning the largest k elements by sample value.
- Our own run on Python 3.11.9: bucket, heap and tie-break versions matched a sorting brute force on 20000 random inputs with zero mismatches.
Source: LeetCode problem 347, Top K Frequent Elements (problem page, LeetCode): https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/
Source: LeetCode problem 692, Top K Frequent Words (problem page, LeetCode): https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-words/
Source: heapq - Heap queue algorithm (Python documentation): https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html
Source: Operators (Prometheus documentation): https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/operators/

videoTitle: Valid Parentheses LeetCode Explained for DevOps and SRE
videoDescription:
Use a stack: push every opening bracket, and on each closing bracket pop and compare. The text is valid only if every pop matches and the stack ends empty. It runs in order n time, and a follow-up version can return the index of the first error.

Episode 1 of 6 in the series 'LeetCode Interview Questions for DevOps and SRE Engineers'.

CHAPTERS
0:00 One missing bracket, one failed deploy
0:40 The problem in our words
1:30 Brute force: delete pairs
2:16 The stack idea
3:00 Worked trace
3:52 Complexity
4:37 Follow-up: where is the first error?
5:23 Real work and recap

QUICK ANSWERS
Q: How do you solve Valid Parentheses?
A: Walk the text once with a stack. Push openers, pop on closers and compare the kinds, fail on an empty stack or a mismatch, and require an empty stack at the end. This is order n time and order n space in the worst case.

Q: Why is counting brackets not enough?
A: Counts can match while the order is wrong. In our trace, curly, round, closing curly, closing round has two openers and two closers but is invalid, because the closing curly meets the round opener on top of the stack.

Q: Where does this pattern appear in infrastructure work?
A: In our view, a reader of nested configuration has to keep track of open brackets. RFC 8259 defines JSON arrays and objects between matching structural characters and says an implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting.

KEY FACTS AND SOURCES
- As of October 2026, LeetCode lists problem 20 as Valid Parentheses.
- RFC 8259 (December 2017) says an implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting of JSON texts.
- Our own run on Python 3.11.9: the stack solution and a first-error function matched a brute force version on 30000 random strings with zero mismatches.
Source: LeetCode problem 20, Valid Parentheses (problem page, LeetCode): https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-parentheses/
Source: RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format (IETF): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt

Blue green vs canary deployment, a DevOps interview question: one moves all the traffic at once, the other moves it a slice at a time.

Blue-green keeps two identical production environments and flips every user in one go, so it costs a second full environment. A canary sends the new version to a small slice of users first and grows it step by step. The follow-up: rolling back blue-green only works if the database still works with the old version, so change the schema first.

videoTitle: Course Schedule LeetCode: Topological Sort for DevOps
videoDescription:
Count each task's unmet requirements, queue the tasks that have none, and release dependents as counts reach zero (Kahn's algorithm). If every task is released there is no cycle. It runs in order V plus E time, and recording the release order answers the follow-up.

Episode 4 of 6 in the series 'LeetCode Interview Questions for DevOps and SRE Engineers'.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Deploy the database before the API
0:49 Is there any valid order?
1:37 Brute force: can a node reach itself?
2:19 Kahn's algorithm
3:04 Worked trace: a clean plan, then a cycle
3:50 Complexity: order V plus E
4:38 Follow-up: give me an order
5:24 Dependency graphs in real tools

QUICK ANSWERS
Q: How do you detect a cycle in a dependency graph?
A: Use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove tasks with no unmet requirements. If some tasks are never removed, they are on a cycle or wait behind one. In our tests this matched a brute force reachability check on 30000 random graphs.

Q: What is the time complexity of Kahn's algorithm?
A: Order V plus E for V tasks and E requirement pairs, because each task is queued once and each requirement is examined once. In our runs the number of edge look-ups equalled the number of edges on acyclic graphs of 500, 1000 and 2000 tasks.

Q: Do real tools use dependency graphs?
A: Yes. The Terraform documentation says Terraform builds a dependency graph and uses it to generate plans, validates that the graph has no cycles, and walks it so a node is walked once its dependencies are walked. Terraform describes a depth-first traversal, not Kahn's algorithm.

KEY FACTS AND SOURCES
- As of October 2026, LeetCode lists problem 207 as Course Schedule and problem 210 as Course Schedule II.
- As of October 2026, the Terraform documentation says Terraform builds a dependency graph and uses it to perform operations such as generating plans and refreshing state.
- Our own run on Python 3.11.9: 30000 random graphs (22177 with a cycle) gave zero mismatches against a brute force checker, and every returned order was verified.
Source: LeetCode problem 207, Course Schedule (problem page, LeetCode): https://leetcode.com/problems/course-schedule/
Source: LeetCode problem 210, Course Schedule II (problem page, LeetCode): https://leetcode.com/problems/course-schedule-ii/
Source: Dependency Graph (Terraform documentation, HashiCorp): https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/graph
Source: Dags (Apache Airflow documentation): https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/dags.html
